note: Text from the v3 brief: Section 1 (purpose, unit of analysis, place in the DBR design), Section 2 (philosophical commitments) and Section 8.6 (limitations). English only.
thesis: Generative AI and the Organisation of Dental Education (Design-Based Research; pragmatism; institutional theory)
stepLegend: Bracketed codes A1–A10 refer to the implementation steps of the v3 design brief (A1 content architecture, A3 capacity profile, A5 accreditation bridge, A6 practice log, A7 AI coach, A8 this page, A9 research folder). SC1–SC7 are the scenarios.

purpose.intro: The platform exists because of a specific causal chain. Every page, feature and piece of text must be traceable to it.

chain.label: Demand
chain.text: Accreditation bodies are under pressure to specify how AI should be incorporated into dental curricula (Study 1).

chain.label: Gap
chain.text: An international competency framework has existed since 2022 (Schwendicke et al., 2022), yet curricular implementation remains patchy and supplementary (Aura-Tormos et al., 2026).

chain.label: Binding constraint
chain.text: Study 1 indicates that the limiting factor appears to be educator capacity, not student readiness or technology. Most surveyed faculty report no routine use of AI in assessment, and in some samples fewer than 20% understand machine-learning fundamentals (Study 1, Tier 3).

chain.label: Institutional risk
chain.text: Standards that specify student outcomes without specifying institutional conditions may operate only as exhortation (Study 1 conclusion). Under isomorphic pressure (DiMaggio and Powell, 1983), schools may respond ceremonially: documenting AI integration without changing practice. This is the decoupling of formal structure from activity (Meyer and Rowan, 1977).

chain.label: Intervention
chain.text: The platform is designed to build substantive educator capacity and to generate evidence that distinguishes substantive integration from ceremonial integration.

chain.label: Return to accreditation
chain.text: That evidence informs what accreditation standards can reasonably require of institutions, not only of students. This closes the loop back to the accreditation dilemma.

purpose.consequence: The platform must never reproduce the decoupling it studies. Any feature that could generate documentation without practice (certificates, completion badges, "evidence packs" built from self-ratings) is out of scope.

unitOfAnalysis.intro: The thesis studies the organisation, not the individual learner (the education–learning distinction in the methodology chapter). The platform therefore works at two levels:

levels.label: Individual practice
levels.text: how one educator uses AI in teaching. This is the entry point.

levels.label: Institutional conditions
levels.text: the regulative, normative and cultural-cognitive conditions that enable or constrain that practice (Scott, 2014). This is the analytic focus.

unitOfAnalysis.closing: Individual data are only ever a route to understanding institutional conditions. Aggregated, cohort-level views (Part B) are the research unit.

placement.label: Proposed placement
placement.text: Study 7 (faculty development), drawing on Study 1 (scoping review) and the REAL-AI framework paper. [AYMAN TO SUPPLY: confirm placement with supervisors]

placement.label: Status
placement.text: Iteration 0, a conjectural prototype. Studies 2 (interviews) and 3 (survey) are in progress. Their findings must be able to revise the design principles, instruments and scenarios without code changes. This is why all content moves to versioned data files with provenance (A1).

placement.label: Validation path
placement.text: design principles and instrument items go to the Delphi study (Study 5); field use in the pilot (Study 6).

commitments.commitment: Pragmatism: ideas are tested by their consequences in practice
commitments.consequence: Practice evidence is structured as intention → enactment → consequence (A6). Reflection prompts ask what would count as evidence in the educator's own setting.
Instruments are judged by what their use leads to, so each output states what it should and should not be used for (A3).
A second instrument profiles institutional conditions across regulative, normative and cultural-cognitive pillars (A3).

commitments.commitment: Decoupling: formal structure vs actual activity
commitments.consequence: No certificates or badges. "Documented" and "enacted" are kept visibly distinct (A6). One scenario confronts the inspection-pressure dilemma directly (SC3).
The accreditation bridge (A5) shows that the demand comes from accreditation pressure, and warns against copying "AI integration" displays from other schools.
The same content is presented to three audiences (educators, programme or quality leads, researchers and examiners), each with a view suited to them (A5, A8).

commitments.commitment: DBR: iterative, theory-generating, documented design decisions
commitments.source: McKenney and Reeves (2019); Obczovsky et al. (2025)
commitments.consequence: Conjecture map, design principles with provenance, an iteration log, and content versioning (A1, A9).

commitments.source: Khalifah et al. (REAL-AI paper, under review)
commitments.consequence: The four pillars structure the practice instrument and the scenarios. Pillar definitions must be the paper's verbatim definitions (A1).

limitations: Both instruments are draft self-report measures. Validation is planned through expert review (Delphi) and psychometric testing.
Scenario options and their fit ratings reflect the researcher's reading of the REAL-AI framework and Study 1. They are design conjectures for review, not settled judgements.
The evidence base in Study 1 is dominated by attitude surveys and small pilots, so several scenarios address open questions rather than established findings.

The AI coach can be wrong. Its use in a platform about critical AI use is deliberate, but it carries the risk of the automation bias the platform warns against. User ratings of coach feedback are collected to examine this.
Arabic text is a draft translation pending expert review.
In this iteration, no data leave the browser except anonymous score summaries and reflections sent to generate feedback.
